entries: Days and months are travellers of eternity. So are the years that pass by.
Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, opening sentences (trans. Nobuyuki Yuasa, 1966)
Diary

And now let us believe in a long year that is given to us, new, untouched, full of things that have never been, full of work that has never been done, full of tasks, claims, and demands; and let us see that we learn to take it without letting fall too much of what it has to bestow upon those who demand of it necessary, serious, and great things.
Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters 1892 to 1910, to Clara Rilke, Capri, 1 January 1907 (trans. J. B. Greene and M. D. Herter Norton, 1945)
Correspondence
Ring out the old, ring in the new, / Ring, happy bells, across the snow: / The year is going, let him go; / Ring out the false, ring in the true.
Alfred Tennyson, In Memoriam A.H.H., section CIV, lines 5 to 8 (Edward Moxon, 1850; CVI in the final text)
Poetry
In the 1850 first edition the Ring out, wild bells poem is section CIV; it became CVI only after Tennyson inserted two sections in 1851 and 1869. The wording is the first edition’s.
Everything in the world began with a yes.
Clarice Lispector, The Hour of the Star, the opening sentence (Rodrigo S.M., the narrator) (trans. Giovanni Pontiero, 1986)
Fiction
Let no one be slow to seek wisdom when he is young nor weary in the search thereof when he is grown old.
Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius, Lives X.122 (trans. R. D. Hicks, 1925)
Philosophy
Marilla, isn’t it nice to think that to-morrow is a new day with no mistakes in it yet?
L. M. Montgomery, Anne of Green Gables, chapter 21, page 247 (Anne Shirley) (L. C. Page, 1908)
Fiction
Printed as the 1908 L. C. Page first edition has it, to-morrow with a hyphen; the unhyphenated form belongs to a modernised transcription, not to the edition named.
Enlightenment is man’s emergence from his self-incurred immaturity.
Immanuel Kant, An Answer to the Question: What is Enlightenment?, opening sentence (trans. H. B. Nisbet, 1970)
Essay
Rise, brothers, rise, the wakening skies pray to the morning light, / The wind lies asleep in the arms of the dawn like a child that has cried all night.
Sarojini Naidu, Coromandel Fishers, lines 1 and 2, The Golden Threshold (William Heinemann, 1905)
Poetry
The 1905 edition prints a comma, not a semicolon, after the second rise, and titles the poem Coromandel Fishers without the article.
It is perfectly true, as philosophers say, that life must be understood backwards. But they forget the other proposition, that it must be lived forwards.
Søren Kierkegaard, Journals, IV A 164, 1843 (trans. Alexander Dru, 1938)
Diary
Dru’s translation reads as philosophers say, with no article; the popular wording adds the. The Danish entry is Papirer IV A 164 of 1843.
Welcome to the new life!
Anton Chekhov, The Cherry Orchard, Act IV, answering Anya as the family leaves the house (Trofimov) (trans. Constance Garnett, 1923)
Drama
Often quoted as the play’s last line; it is Trofimov’s answer to Anya as the young people leave the house, and Lopahin, Lyubov, Gaev and Firs all speak after it.
Thence we came forth to rebehold the stars.
Dante Alighieri, Inferno, Canto XXXIV, line 139 (trans. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 1867)
Poetry
Men, though they must die, are not born in order to die but in order to begin.
Hannah Arendt, The Human Condition, ch. V, §34, p. 246 (University of Chicago Press, 1958)
Philosophy
In spring it is the dawn that is most beautiful.
Sei Shōnagon, The Pillow Book, section 1, the opening sentence (trans. Ivan Morris, 1967)
Diary
Every limit is a beginning as well as an ending.
George Eliot, Middlemarch, Finale, the opening sentence (1871 to 1872)
Fiction
Now is the winter of our discontent made glorious summer by this sun of York.
William Shakespeare, Richard III, Act 1, scene 1, lines 1 to 2 (Richard, Duke of Gloucester)
Drama
Nothing can ever happen twice. / In consequence, the sorry fact is / that we arrive here improvised / and leave without the chance to practice.
Wisława Szymborska, Nothing Twice, lines 1 to 4, Calling Out to Yeti (1957) (trans. Stanisław Barańczak and Clare Cavanagh, 1995)
Poetry

I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
Henry David Thoreau, Walden, ch. 2, ‘Where I Lived, and What I Lived For’, 1854
Essay
One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, Book Two, Part IV, ch. XII (Childhood), opening sentence, p. 267 (trans. H. M. Parshley, 1953)
Philosophy

But that is the beginning of a new story—the story of the gradual renewal of a man, the story of his gradual regeneration, of his passing from one world into another, of his initiation into a new unknown life.
Fyodor Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment, Epilogue, chapter 2, the closing paragraph (trans. Constance Garnett, 1914)
Fiction
As you set out for Ithaka / hope the voyage is a long one, / full of adventure, full of discovery.
C. P. Cavafy, Ithaka, lines 1 to 3, Collected Poems (trans. Edmund Keeley and Philip Sherrard, Princeton University Press, 1975)
Poetry
The voyage wording is the 1975 Keeley and Sherrard text. Their 1992 revised edition, the one most sites now print, reads hope your road is a long one.
I hope I will be able to confide everything to you, as I have never been able to confide in anyone, and I hope you will be a great source of comfort and support.
Anne Frank, The Diary of a Young Girl: The Definitive Edition, entry of 12 June 1942 (trans. Susan Massotty, 1995)
Diary
For a conscious being, to exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.
Henri Bergson, Creative Evolution, ch. I, p. 7 (trans. Arthur Mitchell, 1911)
Philosophy
A word is dead / When it is said, / Some say. / I say it just / Begins to live / That day.
Emily Dickinson, ‘A word is dead’ (Franklin 278), Poems, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd, Life VI (1896)
Poetry
You are about to begin reading Italo Calvino’s new novel, If on a winter’s night a traveler.
Italo Calvino, If on a winter’s night a traveler, chapter 1, the opening sentence (trans. William Weaver, 1981)
Fiction
A book must be the axe for the frozen sea inside us.
Franz Kafka, Letters to Friends, Family, and Editors, to Oskar Pollak, 27 January 1904 (trans. Richard and Clara Winston, 1977)
Correspondence
Risk! Risk anything! Care no more for the opinions of others, for those voices. Do the hardest thing on earth for you. Act for yourself. Face the truth.
Katherine Mansfield, Journal of Katherine Mansfield, entry of 10 October 1922 (ed. J. Middleton Murry, 1927)
Diary
The 1927 Journal dates the entry 10 October 1922, under the heading The Final Step, and reads opinions in the plural. Later editions redate it to 14 October, her birthday.
Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact.
William James, Is Life Worth Living?, in The Will to Believe, final paragraph (1897)
Essay
Not the essay’s closing sentence: it opens the final paragraph, after Be not afraid of life, and James italicises is, which the card cannot show.
For actually the earth had no roads to begin with, but when many men pass one way, a road is made.
Lu Xun, My Old Home, the closing sentence (the narrator) (trans. Yang Hsien-yi and Gladys Yang, 1960)
Fiction
We shall not cease from exploration / And the end of all our exploring / Will be to arrive where we started / And know the place for the first time.
T. S. Eliot, Four Quartets, ‘Little Gidding’, part V, lines 26 to 29 (Faber and Faber, 1942)
Poetry
The popular wording adds a comma after exploration; Eliot printed none. The text is Faber’s of 1942, collected in Four Quartets in 1944.
One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, closing sentence of the essay (trans. Justin O’Brien, 1955)
Philosophy
Last year is dead, they seem to say, / Begin afresh, afresh, afresh.
Philip Larkin, The Trees, lines 11 and 12, High Windows (Faber and Faber, 1974)
Poetry

unused.quote: Listen to the reed how it tells a tale, complaining of separations.
unused.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book I, line 1 (trans. Reynold A. Nicholson, 1926)
unused.note: Verified opening line. Nicholson later revised it after the oldest manuscript to Listen to this reed how it complains; the 1926 wording ships with the 1926 date. Held for a quieter month.

unused.quote: In a hole in the ground there lived a hobbit.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Hobbit, ch. 1, ‘An Unexpected Party’, first sentence
unused.note: Verified opening line, pure delight; January had more openings than days. Mind the cap: the Calendar For Life bank carries many Tolkien lines.

unused.quote: I am large, I contain multitudes.
unused.source: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass, ‘Song of Myself’, section 51, 1881 text
unused.note: Verified; parenthetical in the source. Not a beginning line so much as a truth-and-clarity line.

unused.quote: A classic is a book that has never finished saying what it has to say.
unused.source: Italo Calvino, Why Read the Classics?, definition 6 (trans. Patrick Creagh, 1986)
unused.note: Verified. Calvino appears in January with the opening of If on a winter’s night a traveler; one person per month.

unused.quote: Our battered suitcases were piled on the sidewalk again; we had longer ways to go. But no matter, the road is life.
unused.source: Jack Kerouac, On the Road, Part Three, ch. 5, closing sentence (Sal Paradise)
unused.note: Verified against fifteen scans of the Viking and Penguin text; it closes chapter 5 of Part Three. A road line, for the month of the Way.

unused.quote: And, when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it.
unused.source: Paulo Coelho, The Alchemist, Part One (Melchizedek, the king of Salem) (trans. Alan R. Clarke, 1993)
unused.note: Verified in Clarke’s translation with the leading And; Melchizedek speaks it. Hope rather than beginning.

unused.quote: yes I said yes I will Yes.
unused.source: James Joyce, Ulysses, episode 18, Penelope, closing words (Molly Bloom)
unused.note: Verified closing words of the novel, lowercase because the sentence runs on. Bloomsday is 16 June.

unused.quote: The only true voyage of discovery, the only fountain of Eternal Youth, would be not to visit strange lands but to possess other eyes, to behold the universe through the eyes of another, of a hundred others, to behold the hundred universes that each of them beholds, that each of them is.
unused.source: Marcel Proust, The Captive, ch. 2, the Vinteuil septet at the Verdurins’ (the narrator) (trans. C. K. Scott Moncrieff, 1929)
unused.note: Verified; the real Moncrieff sentence, not the circulating paraphrase about new landscapes. The full stop is the cut at a semicolon.

unused.quote: Light, my light, the world-filling light, the eye-kissing light, heart-sweetening light!
unused.source: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Song Offerings), poem 57, first line (trans. the author, 1912)
unused.note: Verified in Tagore’s own English of 1912. A light line for the dark month.

unused.quote: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, A Room of One’s Own, ch. 1 (1929)
unused.note: Verified. Woolf’s other survivor, the opening of Mrs Dalloway, is the stronger January line, and neither made the month; one person per month either way.

unused.quote: But man is not made for defeat. A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea, unchaptered, after the first shark (Santiago) (Scribner, 1952)
unused.note: Verified in the 1952 Scribner text; Santiago says it aloud. A courage line.

unused.quote: Barrabás came to us by sea, the child Clara wrote in her delicate calligraphy.
unused.source: Isabel Allende, The House of the Spirits, chapter 1, the opening sentence (trans. Magda Bogin, 1985)
unused.note: Verified opening line in Bogin’s translation; it returns as the novel’s last line. Held for a month that can use a pure opening.

unused.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
unused.note: Verified opening line. Held because January had more openings than days.

unused.quote: Ships at a distance have every man’s wish on board.
unused.source: Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God, chapter 1, the opening sentence (1937)
unused.note: Verified opening line. The paragraph goes on to say some ships never land, so it is hopeful only as a single sentence; place it with that in mind.

unused.quote: We tell ourselves stories in order to live.
unused.source: Joan Didion, The White Album, the title essay, opening sentence (Simon and Schuster, 1979)
unused.note: Verified opening line. The essay goes on to test the claim, so the line is cooler than it reads alone; a truth-and-clarity line.

unused.quote: This book was written in good faith, reader.
unused.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, To the Reader, the opening sentence (trans. Donald M. Frame, 1957)
unused.note: Verified opening line in Frame’s rendering. Good faith belongs with plain speech.

unused.quote: And it seemed as though in a little while the solution would be found, and then a new and splendid life would begin; and it was clear to both of them that they had still a long, long road before them, and that the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning.
unused.source: Anton Chekhov, The Lady with the Dog, section IV, the closing sentence (trans. Constance Garnett, 1917)
unused.note: Verified closing line. Chekhov appears in January with Trofimov’s Welcome to the new life; one person per month.

unused.quote: All men by nature desire to know.
unused.source: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book I, ch. 1, 980a21 (trans. W. D. Ross, 1908)
unused.note: Verified opening line of the Metaphysics in Ross. Held because January had more openings than days.

unused.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.
unused.source: Plotinus, Enneads, I.6.9, On Beauty (trans. Stephen MacKenna, 1917)
unused.note: Verified in MacKenna 1917. A clarity line rather than a beginning line.

unused.quote: If it were customary to send daughters to school like sons, and if they were then taught the natural sciences, they would learn as thoroughly and understand the subtleties of all the arts and sciences as well as sons.
unused.source: Christine de Pizan, The Book of the City of Ladies, Part I, ch. 27, p. 63 (Lady Reason) (trans. Earl Jeffrey Richards, 1982)
unused.note: Corrected to Richards 1982; the little girls wording is Rosalind Brown-Grant, Penguin 1999. Page 63 is the 1982 Persea printing; the 1998 reissue paginates differently. Lady Reason speaks. A justice line.

unused.quote: Had Aristotle prepared victuals, he would have written more.
unused.source: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, Reply to Sor Filotea de la Cruz, the philosophies of the kitchen (trans. Margaret Sayers Peden, 1982)
unused.note: Corrected: trimmed to the sentence confirmed in Peden’s translation; the lead-in clause about trivial details was not checked. The refuter confirmed the wording in the Penguin 1997 reprint, p. 43, which the citation may name instead.

unused.quote: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
unused.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part V, Proposition 42, Scholium, the closing sentence (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1883)
unused.note: Verified closing line of the Ethics in Elwes. A discipline line.

unused.quote: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
unused.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, ch. 4, answering Rousseau
unused.note: Verified in the 1792 text, immediately after the Rousseau quotation. A self-mastery line.

unused.quote: Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.
unused.source: Simone Weil, letter to Joë Bousquet, 13 April 1942 (trans. Raymond Rosenthal, 1976, in Pétrement, Simone Weil: A Life, p. 462)
unused.note: Verified in Rosenthal’s translation as quoted in Pétrement; page 462 rests on four scholarly citations, not the page itself. A kindness line.

unused.quote: Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real.
unused.source: Iris Murdoch, The Sublime and the Good, Chicago Review 13.3 (1959), p. 51; in Existentialists and Mystics (1997), p. 215
unused.note: Verified against the Chicago Review page itself. A compassion line.

unused.quote: Some men say an army of horse and some men say an army on foot and some men say an army of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth. But I say it is what you love.
unused.source: Sappho, If Not, Winter, Fragment 16, lines 1 to 4 (trans. Anne Carson, 2002)
unused.note: Verified in Carson, p. 27. What you love: a February line.

unused.quote: Tell me about a complicated man.
unused.source: Homer, The Odyssey, Book 1, line 1 (trans. Emily Wilson, 2017)
unused.note: Verified opening line of Wilson’s Odyssey. Held because January had more openings than days; a line for hard roads.

unused.quote: Although the wind blows terribly here, the moonlight also leaks between the roof planks of this ruined house.
unused.source: Izumi Shikibu, ‘Although the wind’, The Ink Dark Moon (trans. Jane Hirshfield with Mariko Aratani, 1988)
unused.note: Verified in Hirshfield and Aratani. A stillness line.

unused.quote: No coward soul is mine, no trembler in the world’s storm-troubled sphere: I see Heaven’s glories shine, and faith shines equal, arming me from fear.
unused.source: Emily Brontë, No Coward Soul Is Mine, lines 1 to 4, Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey, with Literary Remains of Ellis Bell (1850)
unused.note: Verified in the 1850 text as reprinted in 1908. A courage line.

unused.quote: You must change your life.
unused.source: Rainer Maria Rilke, Archaic Torso of Apollo, New Poems: The Other Part (1908), closing line (trans. Stephen Mitchell, 1982)
unused.note: Verified closing line in Mitchell. Rilke appears in January with the New Year letter; one person per month.

unused.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
unused.source: Karin Boye, Yes, Of Course It Hurts, lines 1 and 2, För trädets skull (1935) (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
unused.note: Verified in McDuff. Buds breaking: a spring line.

unused.quote: Another heavenly day.
unused.source: Samuel Beckett, Happy Days, Act I, Winnie’s first words after the bell (Grove Press, 1961) (Winnie)
unused.note: Verified opening line, but it is the ironic optimism of a woman buried to the waist, and a VERIFIED line may carry no note. Place it only where the source line can carry the context.

unused.quote: There is always something left to love. And if you ain’t learned that, you ain’t learned nothing.
unused.source: Lorraine Hansberry, A Raisin in the Sun, Act III (Random House, 1959) (Mama, Lena Younger)
unused.note: Verified against the Act III text; Mama to Beneatha. A compassion line.

report.thinnestLane: Drama (4 survivors, 2 usable on the theme; Correspondence the same)
